comparison: Both strongly support the core metabolic phenotypes of trpγ mutants (C4, C7, C22-C29). OpenEval emphasizes the strength of multiple independent alleles and rescue experiments with adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers affirm 'solid evidence' and note confirmation through TAG levels and lipid droplet staining. Complete agreement on these foundational findings.

Both strongly support DH44 neuron specificity for lipid regulation (C8, C31-C41, C48, C133). OpenEval highlights necessity/sufficiency experiments and controls with dILP2 neurons. Peer reviewers praise the 'careful analysis of which cells express trpγ' and note the advancement in understanding neural mechanisms of metabolic stress. Complete agreement on cell-type specificity.

Perfect overlap on lipid droplet staining claims (C45-C47). Both evaluations strongly support the enlarged LD phenotype in mutants, cell-specific rescue, and DH44 inactivation phenocopy. OpenEval notes robust imaging with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers praise the fat droplet staining as strong supporting evidence alongside TAG measurements.

Both strongly support starvation-specific phenotypes (C9-C10, C53-C60). OpenEval emphasizes the distinction between normal lifespan and starvation defects, noting appropriate statistical methods. Peer reviewers accept the starvation resistance findings and rescue experiments without challenge, noting the lipolysis defect interpretation.

Both support AMPK/metformin rescue (C64-C65, C69-C77, C92-C93). OpenEval notes this as reasonable but suggests additional mechanistic validation would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers praise these as 'creative endeavors' demonstrating therapeutic potential. OpenEval is slightly more cautious about mechanistic depth.

Both support metformin effects on TAG and LD size (C69-C77). OpenEval emphasizes dose-dependent effects and time-course data with adequate sample sizes. Peer reviewers highlight metformin's role in demonstrating TRPγ as a therapeutic target. Complete agreement on these pharmacological findings.

Both support bmm downregulation findings (C79-C84, C82-C84, C87-C90). OpenEval notes the interpretation of abnormal starvation response is reasonable despite modest sample size. Peer reviewers accept the lipolysis deficit due to bmm downregulation and rescue experiments. Complete agreement on gene expression data.

Both support the specificity of bmm effect shown by lack of changes in gluconeogenic and lipogenic genes (C79-C80). OpenEval and peer reviewers accept these negative results as supporting the lipolysis-specific defect rather than general metabolic dysfunction.

Both support bmm expression in DH44 neurons systemically regulating TAG (C88-C91). OpenEval finds the tissue-specific rescue experiments particularly interesting and well-supported. Peer reviewers accept the bmm rescue without challenge as part of the lipolysis mechanism.

Both support metformin's selective upregulation of bmm (C92-C94). OpenEval notes this provides mechanistic insight but suggests dose-response and time-course analysis would strengthen conclusions. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the therapeutic potential demonstration.

Both support lipase rescue experiments (C97-C100). OpenEval emphasizes the critical denatured lipase control and notes mechanism remains speculative. Peer reviewers praise these as creative dietary rescue approaches supporting conclusions from multiple angles. Complete agreement on experimental design.

Both support partial rescue by lipid components (C101-C107). OpenEval notes the interpretation about absorption/burning defects is reasonable and highlights important controls. Peer reviewers accept oral administration of TAG and fatty acids as effective rescue. Complete agreement on these dietary interventions.

Both support intestinal lipid accumulation and brain-gut axis involvement (C110-C113). OpenEval emphasizes the strength of brain-specific rescue of intestinal phenotypes. Peer reviewers find the brain-gut axis finding interesting, though co-expression evidence is questioned separately. Agreement on functional brain-gut connection.

Both support DH44R2 specificity (C115-C123, C139, C152). OpenEval notes systematic characterization with mechanistic insight but acknowledges complexity. Peer reviewers accept receptor specificity and the interesting brain-gut axis regulation. Both note DH44R2's unique role is well-supported.

Major disagreement on co-expression evidence (C127-C128). OpenEval supports the immunohistochemistry as providing direct evidence of co-expression. Peer Reviewer 2 specifically challenges this: 'co-expression of trpγ and Dh44-R2 in the gut is not convincing, especially in the picture of the arrows pointing at the autofluorescence signals.' Both accept gut-specific function (C129-C130) but differ on co-localization.

Both support receptor specificity through differential rescue (C124-C126). OpenEval and peer reviewers accept the tissue-specific knockdown experiments as important for establishing gut-specific function. Agreement on functional receptor specificity.

Both support the overarching conclusion about DH44 neuron necessity and sufficiency (C131-C136, C133). OpenEval characterizes this as metabolic syndrome with strong support from phenocopy experiments. Peer reviewers praise the identification of biological meaning and neural mechanisms. Complete agreement on central conclusions.

OpenEval rates the afterdepolarization mechanism (C137-C138) as UNCERTAIN, noting it's speculative without direct electrophysiological evidence in the current study. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this mechanistic speculation.

Both support independent function in brain and gut (C139-C141). OpenEval emphasizes parallel phenotypes and independent rescue as important findings. Peer reviewers accept the dual tissue function, though note incomplete mechanistic understanding. Agreement on multi-tissue action.

Both rate as UNCERTAIN the inconsistency between Dh44Mi TAG levels and LD size (C148-C152). OpenEval notes honest acknowledgment of data complexity requiring further investigation. Peer Reviewer 2 suggests incomplete mechanistic understanding and need for further investigation of cell types. Agreement on this limitation.

OpenEval rates speculative mechanistic proposals (C153-C154) as UNCERTAIN, noting they are plausible hypotheses requiring experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these mechanistic speculations.

OpenEval identifies 24 claims as established scientific knowledge providing context (C1-C2, C5-C6, C15-C16, C19, C44, C49, C62-C63, C66, C78, C85-C86, C95-C96, C108-C109, C114, C143, C157, C179, C182). These are not novel findings and peer reviewers do not separately evaluate background/contextual claims.

Partial overlap on trpγ specificity among TRP channels (C21, C24-C26). OpenEval emphasizes multiple TRP mutant screens as part of core phenotype characterization. Peer reviewers accept trpγ specificity and carbohydrate phenotypes from previous work. Agreement on channel specificity.
Both support non-sex-specific nature of phenotypes (C42-C43). OpenEval notes this is appropriately documented. Peer reviewers accept without comment. Minor finding with complete agreement.

Both support normal lifespan under fed conditions (C50-C52). OpenEval emphasizes this distinction strengthens interpretation of starvation-specific lipolysis defect. Peer reviewers accept this as consistent with the metabolic phenotype. Agreement on specificity of starvation effects.
Both support lack of protein regulation changes in receptor mutants (C118). OpenEval and peer reviewers accept this as consistent with lipid-specific role. Agreement on metabolic specificity.

Peer reviewers accept the inability to identify cells regulating protein homeostasis (C134, C164) as a limitation. Reviewer 3 notes lack of explanation for non-cell autonomous function. OpenEval does not separately evaluate this negative result, though it's included in the broader context claims (R20).
